I think the argument is more about the free exercise clause of the 1st amendment rather than the free speech clause of the 1st amendment.

The constitutional counter here is the 14th amendment (state checks on equal protection and due process) because Oregon has an anti-discrimination law on the books that bars discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations including the provision of goods and services.

Alright so the rights being referred to are based on the Federal Religious Freedom Restoration Act. Under FRFRA, laws that “substantially burden a person’s exercise of religion” will not stand, unless the government can show that the burden is necessary in order to further a “compelling governmental interest” and that achieving that interest is done in the “least restrictive” way possible. That legal standard is known as “strict scrutiny.”

This was passed in the 90's in response to a Supreme Court case involving Native Americans and smoking some peyote. (Employment Division v. Smith) FRFRA has more with shoring up protections for those less widely practiced religions whose unusual rituals, might otherwise be rendered illegal.

Now originally people thought FRFRA applied to states as well but in like 1997, the Supreme Court said it didn't. So a bunch of states passed a state version of this.

Does this mean there should/will be a legal debate about how the anti-discrimination laws affect the Religious freedom laws? Or are the lines pretty well drawn? The state sided with the customers in this one. Is that probably what will happen in most cases like this?

So I think a lot will go to how judges apply strict scrutiny.As I said before its kind of a balancing of interests.

Where it’s illegal to discriminate, a religious-freedom defense requires proving that the antidiscrimination statute “substantially burdens” religion. (i.e. is this law preventing me from practicing an essential component of religion?) Even if it does, courts routinely conclude that preventing discrimination is a compelling interest, so the LGBT plaintiff wins.

Now that I think of it, activities with a strong expressive component (i.e. officiating or singing at a wedding) may claim that their First Amendment free-speech or association rights trump antidiscrimination statutes. Some of these claims may prove successful but it will come down to the application again of strict scrutiny.

Finally state and federal law allows individuals to refuse to provide certain services, such as abortions, based on moral objections. Similar conscience-based protections may eventually be demanded to accommodate moral objections to participation in same-sex weddings by the likes of wedding planners, photographers or bakers. Although I'll admit you never want to try to apply abortion laws outside of abortion cases... no rhyme or reason anywhere.

Without any other evidence, discrimination will be hellishly difficult to prove but you've clearly violated the law.

It's not so much a free speech issue as it is a freedom of association issue. Do we really want to get into forcing people to contribute to causes and events they don't agree with? Look, I think these bigots are assholes, but this kind of thing can go both ways. Should gay business owners be forced to provide their labor for bigoted Church conferences and events? I hope not.

I am thinking about making a chicken hut. I was wondering how many I should get. I also have questions about how much it will cost to feed them and any other costs.
How many chickens would i need to get 12 eggs a week?

A chicken lays one egg per day. So, two birds will make 14 eggs a week. That said, they're social birds, so you may want to get a couple more than that (four total) for the sake of their well-being (plus redundancy and all that). A sack of feed every couple of months will run you roughly 15-20 bucks for the organic good stuff.

Almost one egg per day.

I'd say 12 eggs a week to be safe, but also need to account for moult :)
Also...Breed matters. I've got a Leghorn that lays 6 eggs a week. My Easter Eggers lay about 4 or 5 a week on average.
I base my calculations on average you will get 2 eggs every 3 days from one bird. As mentioned earlier, season (length of daylight actually) and breed will effect their day to day productivity.

You need to consider is breed, time of year (season), molting, age and stress.

We started with 15 hens and once they got to laying, we were getting 12-13 a day. Now we have 23 hens total (12 from the original 15) and we're only getting 7-8 eggs/day right now. Many are going through molting, 12 are 2+ years old now and then my son likes to chase them. Plus, it's getting colder and they don't have as much light per day.

Feeding costs aren't bad, but you need to keep an eye on it. We go through 1 50lb bag of crumble per week with 23 hens and 2 roosters. We prefer pellets, but our roosters are scissor-beaks and can't eat the pellets.
